en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Pō’ān:
The True Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is, at its inception, not something that can be transmitted. That which *can* be transmitted is merely the trap and the snare.

Nevertheless, when the lineage of teacher and disciple is authentic and the fundamental roots are clearly discernible, then whether there are words or no words, they are none other than the True Dharma. It is for this reason that [the teachings] are brought forth and propagated.
The Patriarchal Way has been revealed to later students so that people may follow the finger to see the moon; how could it be without transmission?
The late Master Pò'ān previously occupied nine seats of the Dharma, speaking words of no meaning that stood like a thousand-fathom cliff—steep, precipitous, and towering.
In his teaching and practice, he was both expansive and penetrating; he shattered the hidden snares of Miam. His conduct was lofty and steep, far continuing the ancestral style of Foguo.
When he fully raised the true command, all quarters were swept away by its influence. Through his great capacity and secret function, even non-Buddhists vanished from his path.
He alone wielded the hammer and tongs of the fundamental school, forging and refining countless Zen monks. Among the masters of recent times, few could equal him. Alas! In these present days...
At a time when the Dharma is weak and Māra is strong, we relied upon you as a single pillar to stem the surging tide of decline;

now that you have passed away, where shall future students look for guidance? Although I have not personally beheld the Master’s countenance, through our exchange of letters and discussions on these matters, we shared the same spirit across a thousand li, as if joined by a tally and seal.
Now, your attendant Yuanzhao has compiled your recorded teachings and requests a preface for their publication.

I have read and contemplated this again and again; it is not merely that I feel as though I have met him face-to-face, but I have also captured his very spirit. Thus I know that the Elder Pò’ān is not yet extinct.
Is the continuation of the Buddha’s wisdom-life not found in these writings? Those who study the Way and seek excellence must possess the true eye.
Written respectfully by the layman Yangzi of Haozhai on the first month of summer in the Ren-shen year of the Jiading era,
as the preface to the catalog of the recorded sayings of Master Po’an.
Preface (by Yang Haozhai):
*The Recorded Sayings of the Xianping Chan Monastery on Sleeping Dragon Mountain in Kuifu* and *The Recorded Sayings of the Xiufeng Chan Monastery in Pingjiangfu*.
Recorded Sayings from Guangshou Huiyun Chan Monastery in Lin’an Prefecture;
Recorded Sayings from Qionglongshan Fuzhen Chan Monastery in Pingjiang Prefecture;
Recorded Sayings from Fengshan Zifu Chan Monastery in Huzhou Prefecture.
Record of the Discourses at Xianping Chan Monastery on Wolong Mountain in Kuifeng (Appended: Postscript by the Dharma-nephew Fuzhen, Daoyan);
Verses of Praise and Biographical Account of the One Who Grasped the Whisk and Universally Expounded the Dharma.
The monk Yuanzhao and others, students of the Way, compiled this for entry into the monastery.

Pointing to the triple gate, he said: "This is the Great Gate of Liberation. It is the dwelling place of those who have transcended views and surpassed emotions, who are without desire and without dependence. Ha! For now, stay outside the gate."

Pointing to the Dharma-seat, he said, "The emptiness of all dharmas is the seat; dwelling upon this, I shall preach the Dharma. Then he added, "One must indeed place a head atop a head," and ascended the seat.
He then held up the incense and said, "This single offering of incense is respectfully offered to extend the holy longevity of the present Emperor—ten thousand years!
Ten thousand years! Ten thousand times ten thousand years! May his sagely brilliance exceed [the heavens]..."

The sun and moon; his sagely calculations equal those of heaven and earth. He further said, "This single offering of incense is respectfully offered for the sake of the Honorable Grand Councilor and Pacifier, the Tai Zhong, as well as all the honored officials of this prefecture.

May you forever assist the enlightened sovereign and long abide in your positions of rank and emolument. Again, he took up incense and, looking toward the assembly, asked, "Do you know where it falls? The kalpa..."

Even solid rock will eventually crumble; this heart’s bitter resentment is difficult to forget. I offer this in honor of the Great Monk Mian, currently residing at Tiantong Jingde Chan Temple in Mingzhou, to repay the milk of the Dharma.
He then took his seat and said: "One who can skillfully wield the Great A-sword will surely avoid the calamity of injuring their hand;
one who can stroke the whiskers of a fierce tiger must possess the strategy to turn back. Is there anyone [who can do so]?
"Without wounding the tip or offending the hand, is it so? A monk asked: "The robe and bowl were personally transmitted in former days; your renowned fame has topped the four Sichuans.
Limitless humans and devas all lean their ears—please, Master, offer one phrase to bless the Emperor’s long reign. The Master said: "The Twelve Peaks of Mount Wu. The monk pressed further:
"Everyone knows how to offer prayers for the Imperial Throne; but when the General's banner arrives at the banquet, what is the matter?"
The Master said, "The pure breeze comes and does not cease. The student asked, "If Boya did not meet Ziqi, how could his lofty melody have reached the nine realms?
The Master said, "It blocks the faculty of hearing. The student asked, "The one path above, which the thousand sages do not transmit—why was the robe transmitted at midnight at Huangmei?
The Master said, "At that moment, there was no time for hesitation. The student asked, "Since there are already seven..."
"Among the hundred eminent monks, why did he entrust his robes and bowl to the Layman Lu? The Master said, "How many people's eyes have burned with envy!
A student stepped forward and asked, "When the Venerable Ming pursued him to the top of Dayu Ridge, why was he unable to lift them up? The Master said:
Not only did Ming Shouzhuo speak thus; he further said, "Venerable Master, I have not come for the sake of robes, but have specifically come for the sake of the Dharma.
I beg you, practitioner, to grant me instruction. What was the meaning of this? The Master said, "That is not yet a good mind.
He further asked, "Just as the practitioner said, 'Do not think of good, do not think of evil'—at that very moment, what is the original nature of Venerable Ming?"
"Come forth and show me your original face; if you understand clearly, you will immediately awaken. Is there anything definitive about this? The Master said, "Three lifetimes and sixty kalpas.

The student stepped forward and said, "When you see the moon, cease looking at the finger; once you have returned home, stop asking about the journey. The Master responded instantly, "What is your home?"
The monks prostrated. The Master said, "It is indeed quite similar. He then continued: "Mist shrouds the vast sky; wind stirs the great fields.
The splendor of spring overflows the eyes, and the myriad species flourish in glory. Having finished traveling through hundreds of cities, one ascends directly to the Precious Abode.
Therefore it is said: 'I originally had no mind to seek anything; now this treasure-store has arrived spontaneously. Above is heaven; below is earth."

Now tell me, where is the Treasure Store? If you can see it here, then you have seen it. The Prefectural Governor and Pacifier wields the power of creation and upholds the discourse of impartial justice;
he has pointed out the mountain-climbing axe from atop his hair-tip brush, so that those with eyes may see and those with ears may hear.
Hearing and seeing are distinct and clear. What serves as proof? He points with his staff and says: "Look!"
To clarify the impartial phrase of Shaoshi is itself the heart of benefiting beings within the Yellow Hall. Again, it is cited:
Magu asked Linji, "Of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, which one is the True Eye? Linji said, "Of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, which one is the True Eye?
Magu dragged Linji down from his meditation seat and sat back down. As Linji stepped forward and said, "How do you do? Magu hesitated.
Ji then pulled him down from the meditation seat and sat back down. Gu stepped out, shaking his sleeves.

The Master said, "The mechanisms of these two great elders were like crashing thunder and their eyes like shooting stars; yet they could not avoid being seen through by an onlooker. But tell me, who was the onlooker?
After a long silence, he said, "I have stood here for a long time, honored guests. I pray you take care."
The Head Administrative Officer, Xie, ascends the hall: Upholding the True Dharma Eye of Linji, He extends his hand to that person of courage and resolve.
Benefiting beings and responding to conditions with his entire being— Once again, a new chapter is seen within the monastic groves.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised [this koan]: "The mind-moon is solitary and full; its light swallows the ten thousand phenomena. The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist.
When both light and objects are forgotten, what is it then? The Master said: "The ancient sages, in their single act of compassion, could not avoid dragging through mud and water.
Wolong, however, is not like this: when light and objects are both forgotten, one must take care not to mistake the bell for a jar."
Ascending the hall, he said: "When one sees smoke from across a mountain, one knows it is fire; when one sees a horn from behind a wall, one knows it is an ox.
He then took up his staff and said: "This [staff] does not separate us by even a hair’s breadth. What, after all, shall we call it?
Sometimes it leans against an ancient screen, allowing brush and ink to enter the painted picture."

Upon receiving the news of Miman’s passing, he ascended the hall and said: "A guest comes from the south, reporting that the old man of Tiantong has broken through the vast void and entered whole and entire into the wild weeds.
Now, if one considers this carefully, it leaves people unable to weep and unable to laugh.
Vast and empty, the thousand peaks are revealed at dawn."

A Small Lecture for the End of the Summer Retreat: Before leaving Tuṣita Heaven, he had already descended into the royal palace; before emerging from his mother’s womb, his work of saving beings was already complete.

This is already like tracing a pattern from a mold. Yet, he could not help but ride the fragrant elephant of the sun-wheel to manifest birth in the royal palace, scale the city walls at midnight, and undergo six years of ascetic practice.
Eventually, he spread a net across the heavens and cast a hook ten thousand *li* long, to strike the phoenix and snare the dragon.

The Dragon adapts to circumstances according to the vessel, like a seal transmitting a seal, or like space containing space. He fully manifests the local scenery of the original ground and reveals the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye;
he does so with such disregard for others that even those who sit by the stump waiting for a rabbit take it to be the reality.
Little do they realize that within the armory of our King there is no such sword. This is for those of keen faculties and superior wisdom.
One never, even for a moment, lapses into tasting the flavor within, seeking understanding through intellectual interpretation, or engaging in the weighing and measuring of progress and retreat.
One turns everything upward and downward until it is utterly overturned; empty-handed, one grasps at the void. It cannot be caged, nor can it be called back when summoned.
One scatters dust and soil, flies sparks and spreads fire—seeking out grievances and enemies—and yet still has not even a faint semblance of it. Is this not so?
The Path of Seeing: the Mysterious Gate has no dharma; it establishes no regulations. If you wish to seek it out, realize it before a sound is uttered.

Now that the three periods have reached their completion—having spent ninety days sitting, reclining, and walking—exert yourself in mindful cultivation and realization. Once this cultivation and realization are finished:
"The Brahma-faring is established. But how shall one explain the principle of "realizing it before the sound"? One may well envy those guests in a hall of no affairs;
lying deep within the clouds, they do not court the imperial court.
Again, it is recorded: Jinfeng asked a monk, "Do you know Jinfeng’s single phrase? The monk said, "I have known it for a long time.
Jinfeng said, "How so? The monk then gave a shout and said, "Jinfeng’s single phrase—today it is shattered into a hundred pieces!"
Jinpeng said, "I have asked others about this before; among them, the teaching style of the Acharya was particularly steep and formidable.

The monk said, "It is not that one requires someone else to examine it. Jinpeng said, "Brass does not equal gold. Later, Yuanwu said, "Jinpeng dragged through the mud, and this monk waded through the water.
Although he was earnest at the end, he could not avoid missing the mark right at the beginning. The Master said, "The mountain is moist, and the rocks are damp."
The mountain holds its jade; the forest’s Xiuyuan stores his pearls. Pearl and jade shine upon one another; where feelings reach their limit, meaning is difficult to exhaust.
Why, then, do you say he has missed it right before him? When the road is long, one knows the strength of the horse; when years have passed, one sees the heart of man.
Ascending the hall: "The ninety days of this summer retreat have now happily concluded. As for the matters of two thousand years ago, you must strictly avoid seeking them further.
Ascending the hall:
He cited the story of Master Zihu, who in the middle of the night called out loudly before the monks' hall, "Catch the thief! Catch the thief!"
The assembly all started in alarm. Zhaozhou then grabbed hold of a monk and said, "I’ve caught him!
I’ve caught him! The monk said, "It wasn't me. Zhaozhou said, "It was indeed you; it’s just that you were unwilling to take responsibility. The Master [Xuedou] comments:

"Purple Zhaozhou only knew how to startle the crowd and stir the assembly, peddling his cleverness and boasting of his brilliance, without regard for onlookers, thereby inviting his own retribution. Why? Because he falsely accused [the monk]."
The offenses of men are meted out with punishment.
When ascending the hall, Deshan’s staff becomes a mere imitation of a mold or a painted likeness; Linji’s shout turns into nothing but distress.
It is laughable that the "True Person of No Rank" enters and exits through the gates of the face, yet loses his old worn-out sandals for many years.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an ancient case: A monk asked Yantou, "What is it like when one encounters a fierce tiger on the road?
Yantou said, "Press! The Master said: "Yantou’s single press causes empty space to shatter. This is not something transmitted from father to son; it is the secret instruction of the immortals."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this case: For a long time, Yaoshan had not ascended the hall. The head of the monastery said, "The assembly has long been longing for the essential Dharma.

Yaoshan said, "Strike the bell. As soon as the assembly had gathered, Yaoshan returned to his quarters. The head of the monastery followed him to the quarters and said, "Master, you promised to preach the Dharma for the assembly;
why have you failed to utter a single word? Yaoshan said, "For the sutras, there are sutra masters; for the treatises..."
There was a master of the treatises who, being contentious, took offense at the old monk. The Master said, "Yaoshan went straight back to his quarters;
he was like a good man indeed, yet as soon as the attendant struck him a light pinch from behind, he immediately forgot what came before and lost track of what followed."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The heat of summer still blazes fiercely; we rejoice to see the arrival of autumn. Panlang rides his donkey backward; the Brahmin turns his socks inside out.
Truly pitiable and truly laughable, singing and responding all by himself. Sometimes riding upon the bright moon, he passes directly through the blue mists of the sea."
Ascending the hall, he said: "We all dwell together and eat a stalk of radish. It is boiled until soft and steamed until tender. Coarse food satisfies easily; chewing finely makes one hard to hunger.
It is plain and lacks flavor; from of old, few have known it. He struck his knee once and said: "To whom is this meaning clearly explained?"
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an ancient precedent. A monk asked an old master, "When the myriad objects of the world come to invade you, what then? The master replied, "Sit and settle them.
The Master [Zhaozhou] said, "Although that old master had a backbone made of iron, he was not without effort.
If someone were to ask me, Wolong, 'When the myriad objects of the world come to invade you, what then? I would simply say: 'If you do not find it strange, the strangeness will destroy itself.'"

Ascending the hall: Today once again we see the furnace opened; throughout the vast quarters, all is warm and hot. Yet the Dragon’s Lair remains cold and desolate at its gate—this too must be recounted in detail before the assembly.
When night is deep and the watch has ended, there is not even charcoal left; where the patched robe is torn, the ice penetrates to the bone.
The Record of Sayings from Xiufeng Chan Monastery in Pingjiang Prefecture, compiled by the students of the Way, Yuanzhao and others.
Opening the Hall for Teaching. He raised the following: An ancient said, "When Yangqi first settled in, the walls of his house were thin; the entire hall was covered with snow and pearls."
He shrinks his neck and sighs in secret lamentation, turning back to recall the ancients dwelling beneath trees. The Master said: "Yangqi competes for victory, not for inferiority;
Xiufeng competes for inferiority, not for victory. Xiufeng, having newly settled, has no favorites or outsiders; everyone possesses a pearl from the deep blue sea.
Though lakes and mountains fill one's eyes, they can never be seen enough; Śākyamuni and Maitreya are but his servants."
Ascending the hall to thank former acquaintances for visiting: "To encounter a fellow traveler and pass shoulder-to-shoulder—this concludes a lifetime of study.
The Master said, "When the ancient sages spoke thus, it was like falling into a pit on level ground. To encounter a fellow traveler and pass shoulder-to-shoulder..."
This truly falls upon the second pivot of Caoxi. [The Master] struck the meditation seat and said: "Those who have not undergone bitter toil do not know this.
He ascended the hall and raised an example, saying: "Our late master Mian said: 'If asked about the affairs of winter, Beijing produces great yellow [myrobalan].
For the sake of a single grain of rice, one loses half a year’s provisions. The Master said: "Xiu峰 does not speak thus. If asked about the affairs of winter..."
In the capital they produce great yellow [radish], yet by seeking only a single grain of rice, one obtains a hundred years' worth of provisions.
If a supervisor says, "Venerable sir, Venerable sir, do not speak of a hundred years' provisions; even half a year would not be too much," simply reply to him:
"If you prepare a heart of resolve, I shall certainly not deceive you."
Ascending the hall: When Mazu ascended the hall and Baizhang rolled up his mat, the true command was not being carried out; he twisted the crooked to make it straight.
Do you know where the old man Xuedou has landed? "Sitting many times at Shaolin, flowers and leaves fall; walking alone on Mount Yuling, heaven and earth are vast."
Ascending the hall, he raised an example: "Fenyang said, 'If you recognize the staff, your studies as a practitioner are finished.
Letan Cheng said, 'If you recognize the staff, you will enter hell like an arrow. The Master said, 'As for recognizing the staff, set it aside and lean it against the wall.'"
Year-End Small Sermon: Do not do one thing; do not rest until two are done. A true man of great stature should act with freedom.
Sweep away all prior intellectual understandings; overturn the tangled vines of the "path. Do not value your own spirit; do not seek even the sages.
Without reliance and without desire, without joy and without sorrow—always thus, cold and silent, in vain and indolent. It is better to settle upon what you see.
Toward the level fields and shallow grasses, he casts three and releases two; let it simply follow the current as it flows.

How much more so when misfortune reaches its limit and prosperity arrives—spring winds fill the wilds, the radiance of the season overflows the eyes, and the myriad phenomena shine forth. Every beat is the command; every thing is newly renewed.
Yet even Bodhidharma’s nine years of facing the wall have not yet reached their full measure; to this day his ailment remains unhealed. Although Linji...
Possessing the single eye, one must not casually conspire with others. Only the Master’s staff—*thwack!*—it has its own provenance.
Full of indignation, he spreads a net across the heavens and lowers a hook ten thousand miles away; he ensnares dragons and strikes down phoenixes, repaying blow for blow and kick for kick.
In every station, one must distinguish between the black and the white; it is simply a matter of valuing a sense of shame and knowing modesty.
Why is this so? If the great ocean were to know contentment, the hundred rivers would surely flow backward.

Again, it is said that one day Master Shuilong went up to the hall, held up his staff, and said, "For twenty years I have lived in the mountains, and I have relied entirely upon the strength of this. At that time, a monk asked, "Master..."
"What power has he attained? The Dragon said, "Crossing streams and over mountain ridges, leaning eastward and leaning westward.

Later, when Zhaoqing heard this, he said, "I do not speak in such a way. The monk asked, "How would you speak it, Master? Zhaoqing took up his staff, set it on the ground, and leaned upon it as he walked.
The Master said, "A sleeping dragon possesses a fine staff; it is a pity that its head is a dragon’s while its tail is a snake’s. Furthermore, he followed Zhaoqing’s lead."
Later, when he patted [the monk’s] shoulder, it was very much like adding spots to a painted tiger. At that time, had he waited for him to say, "What power did you receive from the Master?
and then have taken up his staff and flung it away, one can be certain he would have grasped the clouds and dazzled the mist.

Ascending the hall: "Upward and downward," "fully raising and half-raising," "the wind blows and the grass bends," and "the Dipper turns and the stars shift"—all these are matters of general labor for practitioners throughout the various quarters.
Here at Xiufeng, there is only this: the many years of "Shang Daren" (The Great Person) and "Qiu Yiji" (Qiu Yi).
If you pick it up, heaven and earth lose their luster; if you let it go, even tiles and pebbles emit radiance. But what about when neither picking up nor letting go?
[He strikes the meditation staff. He descends from the seat.
Ascending the hall: The early summer has just arrived; the fragrant breeze begins to fan. Time rushes like a shuttle; ten thousand transformations and a thousand changes occur.
Only this staff—blackened by age, gnarled, and beyond calculation—knows how to say: "The kitchen and storehouse bow to the Sangha Hall; the triple gate pays homage to the Buddha Hall."
Incense is burned on the anniversary of Miman’s death. This venerable one is not one to gamble; he seizes you as soon as you approach and conceals himself as soon as you lean upon him.
With his ghostly face and divine head, he allows no room for deliberation. In the past, I was deceived by him, and to this day my resentment runs deep into my very marrow.
This enmity is difficult to clear; this resentment is difficult to wash away. Placing his hand upon his forehead, he said: "Namo to the True Origin of Fuzhou. Oṃ sulu siri.
He then ascended the hall and said:
"When body, speech, and mind are pure, this is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world. When body, speech, and mind are impure, this is called [the absence of] a Buddha."

"Nirvana. To practice the three-month retreat of "prohibiting the feet" for ninety days and "protecting life" in this manner is entirely like stirring up waves where there is no wind, or gouging flesh to create a wound.
Yet you further say that the past mind cannot be found, the present mind cannot be found, and the future mind cannot be found.
How is this any different from driving a stake into the ground while rocking the oars? It is not like this at all. When a shrimp leaps, how could it ever get out of the measuring basket?
Have you not seen how, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, the butcher Guang'e cast down his butcher’s blade, displayed his eight limbs, and declared, "I am counted among the thousand Buddhas"?
If you pass Xiu Peak, stay outside the gate for now; as for the rest—this one Śākyamuni, that one Yuanhe, and this Buddha—what are they but mere mounds of earth? (He strikes his knee once.)

Ascending the hall on the occasion of the Imperial Birthday: The Way of the Patriarchs is continuous; the Way of the Kings is level and plain. Together we sing of the Sun of Shun; together we rejoice in the Age of Yao.
His Way penetrates the boundless realms of all lands; his Virtue unifies the vastness of heaven and earth. But how shall this man of the forest retreat repay such grace?
Thereupon he rose and said: "Ten-thousand years! Ten-thousand years! Ten-thousand ten-thousand years!"
Opening the furnace, he ascends the hall. He cites Zhaozhou’s saying: "When I was traveling in the south, there was a 'no host, no guest' koan at the hearth that no one had ever brought up.
The Master says: "Old Zhaozhou, so advanced in years yet lacking in virtue—how little he knew!
That the 'no host, no guest' koan at the hearth shines forth before one's very eyes; its hearing and seeing are vivid and distinct. Earth..."
The wilderness is vast and sparsely populated;

those encountered are few. Entering the hall: to open one’s mouth is already an error; to conceive a thought is already a deviation. Carrying one’s straw hat upside down and wearing one’s robe with the lapels turned backward—look, look!
As the evening sky is about to snow, everyone must take care during the communal labor. But tell me, what is it that you are taking care of? He himself says: “Illumination.”

Looking back at the firelight, he ascended the hall and said: "If you wish to clarify this matter, if you say there is a principle, you are deceived; if you say there is no principle, you are deceived;
if you say it is neither existent nor non-existent, you are still deceived. Why? Because unless you are one who can play in the tide, do not enter the surging waves."
[The Master] entered the hall. On the festivals of Cold Food and Qingming, the spring light reflects upon the forest thickets. Those who mark the graves upon the mounds shed blood from their eyes.
Birth and death are fundamentally traceless; people of this age should resolve this for themselves. Do you not see that the flooded waters have already passed over the horses?
The Master stepped forward. "Right up until this very day, he cannot stop laughing.
He ascended the hall and said, "Today is the fifth day of the fifth month, the Dragon Boat Festival. There is no need for written talismans or incantations; simply take up this staff."
*Claps the desk once.* He says: "It serves as an iron pestle for subduing demons. Grand Master Chu captured the fierce dragon alive;
Grand Master Zhang rode the wild tiger backward. He overturned the carp of the Eastern Sea until it rained down in torrents."
Ascending the hall: Ninety days of this summer season; today, joy is complete. He picks up a tea jar from Gongxian and shatters a magnetic bowl from Raoyou.
With a cold laugh, he treats Pucheng and Lankuan as equals. Neither heaven nor earth can constrain him; neither hell nor purgatory can hold him.
Empty-stomached and high-minded, he carries a mere wooden board; for no reason at all, he blinds the eye atop his head.
The Master ascends the hall to thank the Librarian. He cites a precedent: Once, there was a monk sitting in the library (the *zàngdiàn*).

When the Librarian saw him, he asked, "Why, Senior Monk (*zhùzuò*), do you not read the scriptures? The monk replied, "I do not know how to read. The Librarian said, "Why do you not ask someone else? The monk...

He then rose slowly, folded his hands, and asked, "What character is this? The Librarian was speechless. The Master said, "From the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past, when faced with this question, there has been no opening for a word.
Do you all understand? At the place where this monk asked, the meaning of the character was brilliantly clear;
the Librarian remained silent, not adding a single stroke to the text. We must acknowledge him as a man of mature virtue. He supported [the monk].

Upholding the True Dharma Eye. On the Mid-Autumn Day, he ascended the hall. At Vulture Peak they spoke of the moon; at Caoxi they pointed to the moon. Xuansha has already been chewing his food to feed an infant.
Hanshanzi, for no reason, further says: "There is nothing with which it can be compared; how shall I be taught to speak?"—Xiu Peak.
"Seeing injustice on the road. Zhuo leaned on his staff and said, "Break through the nest!
Compiled by Chan students Yuanzhao and others from the *Recorded Sayings* of Huiyun at Guangshou Chan Temple in Lin’an Prefecture.
The Master was invited to ascend the seat at Lingyin Mountain. He said: "Śākyamuni’s 'closing the room' already reveals error; Vimalakīrti’s 'refusal to speak' turns into a mess.
Were it not for the eye at the crown of the head being upright, how could one distinguish the black from the white? Therefore it is said:
the mirror has no mind yet takes on images, and beauty and ugliness are naturally distinguished; the sword has no intent yet seeks out people, and killing or bringing to life is self-evident."
To manifest benevolence and conceal utility—this must surely be the ultimate principle.
To proceed in this manner, Layman Bian'en has newly established a jeweled monastery to perpetuate the life of wisdom and benefit all beings; one could say his merit is not bestowed in vain.
Yet, should this still not be so, as the saying goes: "Wherever there is a path to ascend, those who excel others will also walk it."
Again, it is recounted: Once there was an official who invited the two masters, Mīkang and Baoshou, for a vegetarian feast.
The official said, "I invite these two elders to discuss the Buddha-dharma. Baoshou said, "I invite my senior brother, Master Mīkang, to provide the answer. Mīkang then gave a shout.
Shou said, "I have never asked that; why did you shout? Cang replied, "You still consider it too little. Shou then followed the sound with a shout of his own.
The Master said, "Although these two great elders were clear-sighted and skillful of hand, alas, their arrowheads did not meet."
Even if they were to strike simultaneously and hit the mark, in the presence of an official, it would only result in a total failure.
Tell me, what kind of discerning eye does the official possess? "Familiarly passing before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion, hand in golden whip, celebrating peace."
He entered the hall. Having ascended the seat and offered incense to pray for the longevity of the Emperor, he next held up incense and said:

"I offer this on behalf of the great patron of the monastery, Layman Yican, and all his noble family members, to increase their years and prosperity. He then took his seat and said: "Words do not unfold the matter;
speech does not meet the occasion. Those who rely on words perish; those who linger in phrases are deluded. Is there anyone here who is completely liberated? A monk [stepped forward].
Question: "The breaking of hermitages and the forging of bellows are few in all quarters; the gates of the lay practitioner’s courtyard stand open in eight characters.

It distributes the treasures of the renunciant life to perpetually sustain the sons of the Buddha, accomplishing inexhaustible Buddhist deeds and establishing a magnificent model for ten thousand ages. Such a person is called a truly eminent Great Man.
Capable of performing rare deeds both mundane and supramundane, he thus manifests coming and going from the root of non-abiding;
within that which is without coming or going, he manifests birth and death in common with others. As for the person who possesses such majestic and formidable skillful means—where is he now?
The path on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is as level as a whetstone; the moon-door is unoccupied, cold as autumn. Furthermore, it is said:
The verse says: Rare events of the mundane and supramundane Must be revealed by one who exceeds all measure.
Appearing and disappearing, rolling up and unfolding, they startle the world’s dreams; The colors of Mount Penglai are renewed once more.

Ascending the hall, the Master raised [the following]: "The Patriarch Yuanwu said: 'When practicing Chan, practice until there is nothing left to practice; when practicing until there is nothing left to practice, only then have you reached the ultimate.
Later, Master Shuian said: 'When practicing Chan, practice until there is nothing left to practice; when practicing until there is nothing left to practice, you have not yet reached the ultimate.
The Master said: 'Do you see where these two great elders differ? The autumn river holds but one crane; the sound of the mortar..."

At Chuya Qianjia, he ascended the hall and raised the following point from the teachings: "All that has form is entirely illusory. He then took up his staff and said, "If you say it exists, then there are phenomena outside the mind.
If you say it does not exist, then the mind's dharma is incomplete. How can you express this?"
Just so. *Zhuo* (a sharp strike). He said: "The sword has long since departed.
Ascending the hall to receive the title of Master of the Secret Seal, he did not sit upon the Palace of the Empty King, nor did he don the garment of original nature.

Why need one act further in this way? One must strictly avoid [discussing] the time before birth. He also said: "Holy names and mundane titles are all but empty sounds; sublime forms and inferior appearances..."

All forms are but illusory colors; it has always been thus. The land is vast and the people sparse; I have merely conformed to custom and blended with the light to maintain a single thread of continuity.

As for me, one of mountain and valley disposition, I was destined to decay along with the grasses and trees. Yet, who would have thought that the grace of Yao’s heaven would fall as rain, moistening these withered remains?
This is because the Commander-in-Chief and the Imperial Guard Officer have not forgotten their entrustment, thereby allowing this wild man of the forest to harbor such an intention.
I am deeply moved and filled with gratitude for Your Majesty’s gracious reception. He further spoke in verse:

"This lone monk with his hanging white hair, In one lifetime has twice received the Imperial Grace. Relying solely on the impartial words of Shaoshi, May he pray for the Sage Ruler, as enduring as earth and heaven."
Ascending the hall on the Mid-Autumn Festival: The moon is full in the heavens; it is half-full among men. If one examines it closely, from the very beginning it has been miscalculated.
Last night, Chang’e lost her golden needle; She shook the Jade Tower, searching everywhere, but could not find it.
Ascending the hall, he said: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. Unable to restrain my impatience, I shall provide you all with a moment of sudden liberation.
He struck his staff once and said: "The flowing water silently erodes the rocks by the stream; I urge people to eliminate the difficulty of right and wrong."

Winter Solstice Small Assembly Sermon. A single stroke of the Chan school cuts off the three baskets of scripture; when the Patriarch’s command is put into action, it severs all paths throughout the ten directions.
Great Master Bodhidharma, his eyes emptying the four seas, crossed the oceans and deserts to see Emperor Wu, yet could only say, "Vast emptiness, no sage.
When asked, "Who is it that stands before me? he replied, "I do not know. With his calculations exhausted and his strength spent, he struck [the Emperor].
He was struck down and killed. He sat there, cold and motionless, before the peak of Shaoshi. One knows not whether he understood or not;
it was for this reason that the Second Patriarch followed him and severed his own arm to find peace of mind.

Having cast off the shell according to the mold, when the time came for verification, he simply performed three prostrations and stood in his place—this is much like the saying, "when cleverness is exhausted, clumsiness emerges. As for the rest—the staff of Deshan, Linji’s...
Huangbo raising his finger, and Bimozha holding up a pitchfork—how could these be worth comparing? Have you not heard it said:

"The emergence of words and traces is the source from which divergent paths arise"? If one can cast one's eye back to the time before the world was established and before the Buddhas and Patriarchs had appeared, only then will one know that light and darkness alternate and cold and heat shift in succession, as the single staff of Shaoshi is fully raised.
The Transmission reveals the moonlight and breeze of our own house; thus one sees the return of the single yang, and the myriad species begin to sprout.

When yin reaches its extreme, yang ascends, and ice forms within water. Furthermore, as for the phrase "participating in the flux of things," how is it so? The Master of the East leaks forth the power of his warm harmony;
even upon branches that have not yet budded, he causes new shoots to emerge.
Again, he raised the anecdote concerning Deshan’s small-scale sermon on the occasion of not answering questions.
The Master said, "Although the old fellow Deshan returned with his integrity intact, he was nonetheless exposed by the monk from Silla."

Ascending the hall on the Winter Solstice: As the season arrives with the recording of the clouds, yin reaches its extreme and yang begins to rise. Flames erupt from the frozen river; blossoms sprout from the withered tree.
Only this staff remains as it was—blackened and cracked, neither shifting nor changing, without disgrace and without glory.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The meanings of the various natures and characteristics—I and the Buddhas of the ten directions alone can know these matters. By day one sees the sun; by night one sees the moon.

Ascending the hall on New Year’s Day: Last year has departed in the night; where did it go? This New Year arrives today; from where does it come?
Since there is neither coming nor going, the iron wall and silver mountains are pointed out as the very core. (He strikes the meditation staff.)

Descending from his seat, he ascends the hall. To extensively seek out knowledge and views is like seeking a form within a mirror; to cease thought and contemplate emptiness is much like fleeing from one’s shadow in broad daylight.

Ascending the hall, he raised [the following] saying: The former sage said, "From ancient times to the present, it has never fallen;

it is clearly before one's eyes. A single cloud arises in the late valley; a solitary crane descends from the distant sky. The willows by the bank are green with mist; the flowers on the crags are fresh with rain.
No one knows this meaning, which makes me remember Nanquan. But tell me, what was the meaning of that ancient one? "The green bamboo sweeps the eaves like a chessboard."
The air is cold; wild clouds enshroud the rocks, and the stone-cotton robe is chill.

The Wisdom of Equality. From the fifteenth day of the fourth month, throughout the worlds of the ten directions—whether grasses or trees, sentient or insentient beings—all practice cultivation and training upon the tip of the whisk.

Now, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, it is released. Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, whether grasses...

Nor is it cramped; it benefits all, so that each obtains what is appropriate for it. Whether they have small roots, small stems, small branches, and small leaves;

or medium roots, medium stems, medium branches, and medium leaves; or large roots, large stems, large branches, and large leaves—the various trees, according to their size and their superior, middling, or inferior natures, each receives its share.
From the rain of a single cloud, they obtain [nourishment] in accordance with their respective seed-natures.

Growing and flourishing—how fortunate that you are so pitiable! When Venerable Kauṇḍinya rose and let out a single shout, you were immediately seen in groups of three and two, unable to maintain your composure; you did not go south of the river, but went north of the river instead.
While it was indeed free and easy for you, suddenly on the way you were intercepted by someone who asked: "What about when there is ten thousand *li* of land without a single inch of grass?"

Transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations, they speak so that emotional dust falls away and conceptual traps are eliminated, until those who sit, those who stand, those who speak, and those who listen are all realized as such.

In the end, one’s entire life passes in vain. As for Old Xue rolling the ball, it has been a source of laughter for people for a thousand ages.

Decide now and act; do not pursue the past. This is precisely the time when the Way of the superior man flourishes and the Way of the petty person wanes;

when yin reaches its extreme and yang ascends, ice forms from water. A man of vast and open spirit should naturally seize this opportunity to gallop like a spirited colt or ride upon a majestic elephant.
It is not that one has not seen the butcher with the broad forehead on Vulture Peak Assembly laying down his butcher’s knife and declaring with noble confidence: [“Today my mind is liberated!”]
I am counted among the thousand Buddhas. Let us set aside for a moment your various displays of shooting stars and scattering fire; they may be evaluated as being either superior or inferior.

Yet how can one distinguish between the monastic and the lay? It is not the hand of Wang Wei; it is merely speaking of painting in vermilion and green.
Again, Huangbo addressed the assembly, saying: "All of you here are nothing but fellows who eat dregs of wine. Traveling on pilgrimage like this, how could you have reached this day?
Do you know that within the Great Tang Empire there are no Zen masters? At that time, a monk stepped forward.

[The Master] asked, "As for those in various quarters who guide their disciples and lead assemblies—how do they fare? Baizhang said, "I do not say they lack Chan; it is simply that they lack a teacher.
The Master said, "Huangbo held authority over the frontier and maintained his commands without violation;

his majestic presence was truly formidable, and he possessed both strategy and tactics in full measure. Yet, when pressed by this monk with such casual ease, he collapsed entirely, prostrate on the ground. The assembly [was moved].
"Is there anyone among you who can act as a witness for Huangbo? After a long silence, he said, "The former senior monk will suffer a fall on level ground tonight.
At the end of the summer retreat at the Head Seat’s quarters of Lingyin Monastery, the Great Matter (the Dharma) emerged from Sheshong; among these matters, that of Fengyi was even more so.
Powerful! Before a question or answer has even taken shape, one must clearly realize it. At the gateway of the six senses, light shines forth everywhere.
To proceed in this manner—when hearing talk of Chan and the Way, it is like the wind passing over the treetops; when speaking of nature and mind, it is like water poured upon a hard rock.
Eyes askance and nose straight, struck by the staff yet never turning back—one is far, far removed from the gate of the Patriarchs. If there were even half a person here who...
This person shall not be deceived; I shall behead myself to offer my apology. Should this not yet be so, then how vast is the height of Heaven and the thickness of Earth!

How brilliant are the sun and moon in their circling course! How boundless are the four realms of birth! A leap month occurs once every three years, and the Double Ninth Festival falls on the ninth day.
This year at Lingyin Mountain, within the community of my Dharma brother, the Abbot, there was neither Chan nor the Way to discuss with others.

During the ninety days of this summer retreat, there was only the single flavor of clear water and white rice, which even the sentient and the insentient were moved to drink thirstily and eat hungrily, all fully realizing the bliss of *dharmaprīti* and *dhyānāsvāda*. Yet, for no reason, the pillar could not bear it and showed its face on every side.
They gaze at one another, weighing and comparing the various Dharma-gates: the Five Ranks of Master and Subject in the Cao-Dong school, and the Four Kinds of Discernment in the Linji school.

These teachings exhaust the profound and reach the subtle; they are most simple and most essential. When the master takes up the whisk to ascend the hall, the disciples step forward with bated breath, bowing their heads and leaning in to listen.
He listened to each point with clear discernment and did not dare to conceal or cover it up as his own possession.
Instead, he explained it from beginning to end before the assembly. After a long silence, he said, "I nearly provided a mistaken commentary."
Again, it is cited: A monk asked Yunmen, "At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, if someone suddenly asks you on the road ahead, how will you respond?
Yunmen said, "Have the assembly step back. The monk asked, "Where does the fault lie? Yunmen said, "Give me back the payment for my ninety days' worth of rice. The Master said:
"One who is skilled in tactical maneuvering examines the source of the matter; Yunmen possesses both the power of total preservation and total destruction."
This command: that monk was bold and coarse-minded; he intended to leap through the Dragon Gate, yet ended up with his forehead scarred. What a pity!
Yunmen’s ninety days of food sat within its own nest, only to be turned into something that follows worldly trends.
If you reach other regions, do not misrepresent this.
I have universally announced the incense-offering ceremony at the quarters of the Chief Seat, Huazang. One of humble and meager standing, I have resided here;

I thought that by relying on the presence of the Abbot, Master Dun’an, my understanding and insight might allow for a life of ease. Yet, I have instead been burdened by the earnest encouragement and guidance of my fellow practitioners.

I have been repeatedly urged to serve as the head of this assembly. Furthermore, at this time, having received the signal of the sounding drum to gather the multitude, you have bestowed upon me excessive praise and encouragement, commanding that I act as a brother to remind others of the *huatou*.
I am deeply ashamed of my own lack of talent; as the saying goes, "If one cannot cure one's own illness, how can one find the leisure to save others?
Yet, as matters have come to this, there is no way to avoid it. I can only comply with your strict command and offer these words for now.
Take this to heart. Moreover, those here are all great practitioners of profound realization from every quarter—men whom no net can ensnare and whom no call can turn back.
They remain here concealing their brilliance and hiding their traces, storing their talents while awaiting the right time. This may truly be described as "the treading of dragons and elephants.
Should you encounter one who hangs up his plaque, do not trouble yourself to visit him; for there might be one or two among the newly initiated brothers whose resolve and effort are insufficient.
Regarding those on the Path, there is no begrudging as you rub and polish one another.

Indeed, in this matter, people see others performing actions, with light radiating from the gates of the six sense organs and shaking the very earth; yet these people themselves remain unaware, instead seeking it elsewhere.
Thus it is said: "Though it is clear, failing to realize it leads to delusion; to whom shall these boundless splendors be entrusted? If one attains the mountain of one's own home...
The field is stable; naturally, everywhere is inconceivable. It is also said: "When this mountain monk was nineteen, I passed by the waters of Lake Tai.
This year I am fifty-two, yet these waters remain as they were, flowing clear on both banks with golden sand spread across their bottom.
When people are turned by external things, their entire being becomes deluded regarding themselves. This is the authentic practice of the former masters who studied Chan.
Thus they realize it and understand it as it truly is. Bringing this forth as the Banner of Radiance, they benefit all beings;
this may be called a model for ten thousand generations and a paragon for a thousand ages. To grasp its essential purpose, one finds it does not transcend the wondrous functioning of the single mind.

Once this wondrous functioning is realized, it is like the wind passing through space, leaving no trace. From the beginning, there is no talk of "I can" or "I understand," nor is there any running about in pursuit.
In this world, one who is ridiculed by the wise has not even a mind remaining; how could there be any Dharma? I once saw a hermitage master in the past.
That master had previously seen the Venerable Master Laocong, who had studied under Huìtáng. Later, [Laocong] was a West Hall Preceptor within the assembly of Zhaòjué Yuánwù.
He would often count on his fingers and say: "From Master Bodhidharma to my late teacher Huìtáng..."
As for this old monk, that man with the "enveloping teeth" has already lost the ability to bend his fingers. This is because Yuanwu’s teeth enveloped his ears; he once held him in deep reverence.
He once composed a Dharma talk to send off a monk on pilgrimage, saying: "This old monk is eighty-two years old. At eighteen, I did not take a wife;
I renounced all conditions to leave the household life. At nineteen, I received the Bodhisattva precepts, and thereafter I have upheld my station."
He attended formal assemblies and traveled on foot for twenty-five years, leaving one monastic community (*saṃghārāma*) to enter another.
He also visited two or three venerable masters in Chengdu, yet he had not yet gained a profound or penetrating realization beneath their words.

Later, upon reaching the presence of the elder Huanglong Huitang, he was questioned regarding the dialogue concerning the wind and the banner; with a single word, he was thoroughly enlightened, whereupon the elder laughed heartily and said:
"You must first seek a point of entry to serve as a foundation; only then can you erect the towers, terraces, halls, and pavilions.
Four years later, he indeed attained entry beneath the Old Man's staff, whereupon he saw that the ten directions were without walls and the four sides were likewise without gates.
It was only after seventeen years from beginning to end that he attained stability. Now, at eighty-two, he is still without it.
I am filled with doubt. Now, Master Qing has suddenly come to bid me farewell, saying: "Human life is impermanent; wealth and honor are like illusions. I have realized this.
Yet he does not realize from where this realization comes, for he now intends to travel throughout the world to investigate its very source.
One should take awakening as the standard. My most sincere wishes! My most sincere wishes! Brothers, have you ever practiced in this way?
Have you ever applied yourselves to the work in this manner? This is a copy of the "Statement of One Who Studies Chan.

It is certainly not like those people of the present day who, being consistently arrogant, treat Chan as something to be carried off with broad strides and long steps, yet whose feet remain utterly without any real grounding. And...
When they reach the point of being relied upon by others, their faces turn blue and yellow again, and they collide with walls and barriers.

You do nothing but strive to understand others, yet you yourself remain in total darkness. Furthermore, you do not realize that all such efforts are merely dung and grease.
